strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem setting: dense semantic scene completion from a single panoramic camera on gait-driven legged/humanoid platforms, a setting genuinely under-explored relative to forward-facing wheeled SSC literature.

Significant dataset contribution: two new panoramic occupancy benchmarks (QuadOcc, a real quadruped 360° capture with day/dusk/night coverage; Human360Occ, a CARLA human-ego benchmark with within-/cross-city splits), accompanied by a broad comparison table of existing SSC datasets (Table 1).

Comprehensive evaluation: strong baseline suite covering LiDAR-based (SSCNet, LMSCNet, OccRWKV), vision-based (MonoScene, OccFormer, VoxFormer, SGN), and LiDAR-augmented vision variants († entries), with per-class IoU, precision/recall, and lighting-condition breakdown (Table 5).

Method is coherently designed around the stated setting: dual-projection encoders (raw annulus + equirectangular), Cartesian/cylindrical bi-grid voxelization, and a lightweight decoder; the 'why it helps' rationale sections tie each module to panoramic or gait-specific characteristics.
Component-wise ablation (Table 4) is clean and shows additive gains; efficiency analysis reports latency, memory, and parameters, with extrapolation to embedded hardware (Jetson Thor).
weaknesses: Headline claim of gait robustness is weakly supported. GDC regresses a single global 2D displacement per scale/projection via GAP over the entire feature map (Eq. 9), which is a very coarse motion model that cannot represent spatially varying gait jitter (foot-strike shocks, roll/pitch). The paper provides no direct evidence linking GDC outputs to actual gait phase/IMU measurements, and no jitter-specific experiment (e.g., training/testing with vs. without gait-induced motion, or displacement magnitude vs. motion amplitude) to validate the central motivation.

Absolute improvement over the best vision baseline on the real dataset is modest: 20.56 vs. MonoScene 19.19 mIoU on QuadOcc (+1.37), and individual ablation deltas are small (0.26–0.41 each). Combined with the semi-automatic ground truth (LiDAR aggregation + Grounded-SAM initialization + manual fixes), it is unclear how much of the margin is meaningful versus annotation-noise level.

The 'surpasses LiDAR baselines' claim needs qualification: it holds only on their own low-resolution (64×64×8, 0.4 m) benchmark with a small 6-class vocabulary and 10 scenes; LiDAR methods were retrained under this setting rather than evaluated at native capability, and this claim does not generalize to standard SSC benchmarks.

H3O is purely synthetic (CARLA), so cross-city generalization gains (+8.08 mIoU) may not transfer to real humanoid deployment; there is no cross-dataset experiment (e.g., H3O→QuadOcc) to bridge the sim-to-real gap despite the paper's framing of cross-morphology transfer.

Presentation issues reduce polish and reproducibility confidence: Figure 2 contains leftover Chinese text ('极坐标转笛卡尔坐标') in the pipeline diagram; the release URL is missing in the abstract; Table 1 has an 'n.a.' camera entry; the AMoE-3D 'expert' design (three fixed 1×1×1 Conv–GELU–Conv experts, K seemingly fixed at 3) is a fairly thin instantiation of the MoE terminology, and several implementation details (encoder backbone, expert count K, cross-grid index construction) are underspecified.
No statistical treatment (error bars, seeds, or variance) for any comparison despite small deltas; training uses a single GPU/seed and val-set results only, with no test split for QuadOcc.

strengths: The problem setting is genuinely under-explored: panoramic (360°) semantic scene completion on legged/humanoid platforms with gait-induced motion is a relevant and motivating gap relative to forward-facing automotive SSC literature.

The paper contributes two new benchmarks (real quadruped QuadOcc and simulated CARLA-based Human360Occ) with a clear comparison table against prior SSC datasets (Table 1), covering day/dusk/night, within- and cross-city splits, which could be valuable to the community.

The experimental protocol is reasonably broad: multiple LiDAR- and vision-based baselines (SSCNet, LMSCNet, OccRWKV, MonoScene, OccFormer, VoxFormer, SGN) are retrained on the new data, and there are component ablations (Table 4) and a lighting-robustness analysis (Table 5).
The paper is generally well organized, with clear motivation sections ('Why it helps') for each module and honest reporting of weaknesses (e.g., OneOcc trails MonoScene at night in mIoU).
weaknesses: The headline claim of gait-jitter robustness is weakly supported by the method actually proposed. GDC (Eq. 9-11) regresses a single global 2D displacement (dx, dy) per scale via GAP + zero-initialized linear layer. A single global shift cannot model the impulsive, spatially varying roll/pitch of gait, and it is applied at sampling time only, so it cannot correct motion blur or inter-frame inconsistency. Moreover, the pipeline appears single-frame, yet the motivation argues that jitter 'breaks temporal coherence' — a single-frame model cannot exploit or test this claim. There is no experiment isolating gait motion (e.g., static vs. moving capture, or correlation of Δs with IMU/odometry), so the central motivation rests largely on assertion.

Gains are modest and possibly within noise. On QuadOcc the improvement over MonoScene is +1.37 mIoU; the individual ablation deltas are +0.39/+0.31/+0.41/+0.26, each of which is small given 24K frames and no variance, seeds, or significance testing. The additive narrative in Sec. 4.3 is not statistically substantiated.

'Lightweight' and 'deployable' claims are not credible as stated: 101.76M parameters and ~70 ms per frame on an RTX 4090 for a small 64×64×8 grid is not lightweight for an onboard legged robot, and the Jetson Thor projection is a crude linear-FLOPS extrapolation rather than a measurement.

SOTA claims are made on the authors' own newly introduced benchmarks, which weakens their evidential value; there is no evaluation on any pre-existing public benchmark to substantiate the method's generality. The 'vision rivals LiDAR' claim compares against a narrow set of somewhat dated LiDAR SSC baselines (SSCNet, LMSCNet, OccRWKV) retrained by the authors, with no evidence these were optimally tuned for the new data.

Ground-truth quality for QuadOcc is semi-automatic (LiDAR aggregation + Grounded-SAM + targeted manual fixes) with no annotation-quality audit (e.g., human verification rate, noise estimates), which matters because all method conclusions are measured against this GT; H3O is fully synthetic with 'simulated gait', so the humanoid claim is only indirectly supported.

The method is largely a composition of known ideas (dual-view encoders, cylindrical/polar voxelization à la Cylinder3D/PointOcc, CBAM-style channel/spatial attention, MoE fusion, zero-init warping) without a clearly identified novel technical insight; the novelty is primarily at the system and benchmark level.

Notably absent baselines/comparisons: no comparison to panoramic/cylindrical occupancy methods cited in related work (e.g., OmniOcc [69], OccCylindrical [71]), and GDC is not compared against obvious alternatives (image stabilization, pose/IMU-based warping, or simply no compensation) to demonstrate it is the right tool.
Reproducibility is currently limited: no anonymized code or data link is provided ('will be publicly available'), calibration details, split definitions, and hyperparameters are only sketched.

Presentation defects undermine polish: Figure 2 contains leftover non-English annotation text ('极坐标转笛卡尔坐标') and 'Sampleing' typos, suggesting a rushed submission; some notation is inconsistent (e.g., v ∈ {equi,raw} vs. {unwrapped,spherical} in Eq. 6 vs. Eq. 11).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: dense semantic scene completion from a single panoramic camera on legged/humanoid platforms with gait-induced motion. This is a well-motivated gap relative to forward-facing, wheeled SSC literature, and the related-work positioning is thorough.

Two new benchmarks constitute a substantive community contribution: QuadOcc (real quadruped, first-person 360°, 24K frames, day/dusk/night, semi-automatic LiDAR-based GT) and Human360Occ (CARLA human-ego 360° with within-/cross-city splits). The cross-city generalization protocol is a sensible addition.

The method is coherently designed around the stated failure modes: dual-projection (raw annulus + equirectangular) encoding, Cartesian/polar bi-grid voxelization, a lightweight hierarchical decoder with MoE fusion, and a gait-compensation module. The 'Why it helps' rationale after each module aids readability.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: LiDAR and vision baselines are retrained on the new data, per-class IoU is reported, lighting-robustness analysis (Table 5) is provided, an additive component ablation is included (Table 4), and efficiency numbers (latency, memory, parameters) are given.
The largest empirical win (+8.08 mIoU cross-city on H3O) supports the claim that the panoramic-aware components improve distribution robustness, which is the most interesting result in the paper.
weaknesses: GDC is under-specified and its mechanism is questionable. It regresses a single global 2D offset (dx, dy) per scale via GAP+Linear, but gait jitter induces spatially varying roll/pitch/perspective error, which a constant per-frame shift cannot correct. Moreover, the paper does not explain what supervises or drives the learned displacement (no motion-prior loss, no gait-phase input), making the 'gait compensation' claim hard to verify. Its ablation gain is the smallest of the four components (+0.39 mIoU).

All evaluation is on the authors' own newly released datasets. There is no experiment on any pre-existing public benchmark (e.g., SSCBench-KITTI-360 with fisheye, which the paper itself lists in Table 1), so the method cannot be externally validated, and the SOTA claims are relative to baselines the authors themselves adapted and retrained on their own data.

Ground truth on QuadOcc is semi-automatic (multi-frame LiDAR aggregation + Grounded-SAM). Claiming a vision-only method 'beats LiDAR-based SSC' on labels generated by LiDAR aggregation is somewhat circular, and label noise likely compresses the margin (OneOcc 20.56 vs. MonoScene 19.19, +1.37 mIoU, with no variance/significance reporting).

Baseline set is dated. The strongest vision comparisons are MonoScene (2022), OccFormer/VoxFormer/SGN (2023), while the paper's own related work cites many stronger 2024-2025 SSC methods ([56-62], [65-68]) that are not compared. The 'new SOTA' claim is therefore scoped to a narrow baseline set.

Ambiguity about the final H3O configuration harms reproducibility and claim precision: the raw-projection branch is disabled on H3O, GDC is described as 'optional on H3O', and it is unclear whether the Table 3 results include GDC. There is also no ablation on H3O, so the generality of the component gains rests on a single small dataset.

The 'lightweight' framing is inconsistent with the reported model: 101.76M parameters, 69.93 ms per frame (≈14 FPS) on an RTX 4090. The Jetson Thor claim is a linear FLOPS extrapolation, not a measurement, and is not convincing evidence of onboard deployability.
Dataset diversity is limited: QuadOcc covers 10 scenes in a single campus domain; H3O is simulation-only. Cross-robot/cross-environment generalization claims are not directly tested.

Presentation needs polishing: Figure 2 contains leftover Chinese text (极坐标转笛卡尔坐标), there are typos ('Quantitatively Comparisons', 'a intermediate layer'), and no public code/data URL is provided at submission time despite the reproducibility promise.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem setting: panoramic, single-camera semantic scene completion for legged/humanoid platforms with gait-induced jitter, a setting genuinely under-explored in the SSC literature; the paper clearly articulates why wheeled/forward-facing assumptions do not transfer.

Two new benchmark datasets with documented construction pipelines: QuadOcc (real quadruped, PAL camera, time-synced Livox LiDAR, Grounded-SAM-assisted semi-automatic labeling, day/dusk/night) and H3O (CARLA human-ego 360° with simulated gait, within-/cross-city splits); detailed GT construction (voxelization, majority voting, OBB handling, quality control) in the supplementary supports reproducibility.

Comprehensive evaluation: LiDAR-based and vision-based baselines are retrained from scratch under a documented, minimal-modification protocol (Sec. 11), and the authors transparently report modality adaptations (e.g., VoxFormer† with LiDAR).

Extensive and honest ablations beyond the main tables: number of MoE experts, FoV scaling (90°–360° with a 'closing-the-ring' analysis), Cartesian vs. cylindrical vs. bi-grid, ER-only vs. raw-only, calibration-noise robustness, temporal aggregation, resolution scaling, distance-binned safety analysis, and a failure-case analysis; the supplementary is unusually thorough.

Deployment-oriented evidence: measured Jetson AGX Orin latency (73.32 ms vs. 98.01 ms for MonoScene) with stage-wise breakdown, plus parameter accounting showing the H3O variant (101.7M) is ~33% lighter than MonoScene (148.9M), supporting the 'lightweight for legged robots' claim.

Consistent and sometimes substantial gains, especially under distribution shift: +3.83 mIoU (within-city) and +8.08 mIoU (cross-city) over MonoScene on H3O, and Pareto-superior accuracy-throughput behavior across FoV settings; calibration-robustness results further support the architecture's geometric consistency.
weaknesses: Gains on the real benchmark (QuadOcc) are modest: 20.56 mIoU vs. 19.19 for MonoScene (+1.37, ~7% relative) and 18.44 for LMSCNet; given the authors designed the benchmark, the tuned method, and its components together, such margins lack statistical support (single runs, no seeds/variance reported), and individual ablation increments (+0.26 to +0.41) are small.

Capacity confound on QuadOcc: the Dual (ER+Raw) variant uses 189.8M parameters vs. MonoScene's 148.9M (+26%), two 2D encoders, and a dual-grid representation; Table 9 shows the accuracy gain from Dual over ER-only is only +0.53 mIoU at +86.5% parameters, so the headline QuadOcc result is not obviously attributable to the panoramic-specific design rather than added capacity.

Ground-truth quality risk on QuadOcc: labels are derived via Grounded-SAM pixel semantics transferred to LiDAR points plus targeted manual fixes; label noise is not quantified (no human-verified subset accuracy, no inter-annotator agreement), which matters because all methods, including the authors', are trained/evaluated on this GT.

Some baseline adaptations appear weak and raise fairness questions: VoxFormer-S performs extremely poorly (9.36 mIoU, below its P+L variant) and VoxFormer†/SGN† variants deviate from original sensor modalities; the paper's own supplementary notes large BEV-PE configurations were infeasible, suggesting the transformer baselines may be handicapped rather than fairly adapted.

Inconsistencies and draft-quality issues reduce confidence: Z bounds are stated inconsistently across baseline sections (e.g., Z∈[−2.0,1.2] in most places but [−12.8,−12.8,−1.2] origins, [−2.4,0.8] for H3O in others, [−1.2,2.0] for OccFormer), leftover non-English text in Figure 2, and typos (e.g., 'inference 40fps ≈ 184.30'); 'robotic occupancy' is undefined in the conclusion.

QuadOcc is small and narrow: 10 scenes within a single campus domain, 24K frames at stride-5 training (effective training set even smaller), and 6 classes; generalization claims beyond campus-like outdoor scenes are untested on real data, and H3O is purely simulated (sim-to-real gap acknowledged but unaddressed).

The GDC module is a very simple global per-scale 2D translation (GAP + zero-init linear, one (dx,dy) per feature map), which is a rather coarse model of gait-induced motion; the +0.39 mIoU gain in isolation is small and there is no quantitative evidence linking predicted displacements to actual measured camera jitter, only qualitative Fig. 8.

strengths: The problem setting is genuinely underexplored: semantic scene completion from a single panoramic camera on gait-perturbed legged/humanoid platforms, with a clear motivation for full 360° situational awareness under payload constraints.

Two new benchmarks are contributed: QuadOcc (real quadruped, PAL camera, semi-automatic GT via LiDAR aggregation + Grounded-SAM + manual fixes, day/dusk/night) and Human360Occ (CARLA human-ego with standardized within-/cross-city splits). The supplementary documentation of the GT construction pipelines (Secs. 9–10) is unusually detailed and supports reproducibility.

The evaluation is extensive: component ablations (Table 4), number of experts and gating (Table 6), FoV ablation 90°–360° (Table 7), Cartesian vs. cylindrical vs. bi-grid (Table 8), projection-path ablation (Table 9), resolution scaling (Table 10), calibration-noise robustness (Table 11), temporal aggregation (Table 12), and measured Jetson AGX Orin latency (Table 15).

Results on the simulated benchmark are convincing: +3.83 mIoU within-city and +8.08 mIoU cross-city over the strongest vision baseline (MonoScene), with a Pareto-superior accuracy-throughput/memory profile across FoVs.

The failure case analysis (Sec. 12.2) and distance-binned safety analysis (Sec. 12.3) are honest and informative, correctly identifying that the remaining errors are largely semantic rather than geometric.
weaknesses: The headline gain on the real dataset is marginal and comes with a capacity confound: OneOcc (QuadOcc configuration) is 189.8M parameters vs. MonoScene's 148.9M (+26%, Table 13), yet improves mIoU only from 19.19 to 20.56 (+1.37). This directly contradicts the 'lightweight' framing of the abstract and Section 8 ('structural lightweight' does not change that the deployed model is larger). The lightweight claim only holds on H3O because the raw-projection branch is disabled there.

The component ablations on QuadOcc are individually small (GDC +0.39, DP-ER +0.31, BGV +0.41, AMoE-3D +0.26) and no seed variance or statistical significance is reported, so the cumulative +1.37 mIoU over the strongest baseline could plausibly be within run-to-run noise.

The GDC ablation is confounded: Section 7 states that the GDC variant also upgrades lifting from integer-index gather to bilinear sampling. The +0.39 mIoU attributed to Gait Displacement Compensation therefore mixes a genuinely different (and known) operator change with the proposed motion model. Given that GDC itself is only a per-frame global 2D shift regressed from GAP features — a very weak model of gait-induced roll/pitch/translation — the mechanistic claim that it 'compensates gait jitter' is under-supported; Figure 8 is a post-hoc qualitative interpretation.

Novelty is largely recombination of established ideas: cylindrical voxelization follows Cylinder3D/PointOcc (acknowledged), dual-view fusion, channel/spatial saliency gates are SE/CBAM-style, and the 'AMoE-3D' is soft MoE over 1×1×1 experts with gradient-energy gating. None of these is analyzed in enough depth to establish a distinct methodological contribution beyond engineering.

The simulated gait in H3O is a simple sinusoidal vertical bob (Eq. 24), which is far from real gait dynamics (impulsive foot strikes, roll/pitch); conclusions about jitter robustness drawn from H3O should be heavily discounted, and the real QuadOcc evidence is the weak +0.39 GDC delta.

The benchmark baselines are dated: the LiDAR comparisons (SSCNet 2017, LMSCNet 2020, OccRWKV) are not representative of modern LiDAR SSC, weakening the 'rivals or surpasses LiDAR' claim; all SOTA statements are relative to the authors' own newly introduced datasets, so external validation is absent.

QuadOcc is small and domain-narrow (10 scenes, one campus, 24K frames), and the GT is semi-automatic; no inter-annotator or label-noise analysis is provided, and label noise could differentially favor the proposed pipeline.

Presentation quality issues undercut confidence: Figure 2 contains leftover Chinese annotation text ('极坐标转笛卡尔坐标'), and the abstract/claims of deployable lightweight perception are inconsistent with the reported parameter counts. Several baselines require non-trivial re-implementation choices (e.g., VoxFormer PE constraints, LMSCNet 8× widening) whose sensitivity to those choices is not quantified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem setting: dense semantic scene completion from a single panoramic camera on gait-driven (legged/humanoid) platforms, where existing SSC pipelines (designed for stable, forward-facing, wheeled setups) do not directly apply. The motivation is well articulated.

Significant dataset contribution: two new benchmarks (QuadOcc — real quadruped 360° with day/dusk/night coverage; Human360Occ — CARLA-based human-ego 360° with weather/lighting diversity and standardized within-/cross-city splits), with a detailed, reproducible GT construction pipeline described in the supplementary (sensor suite, calibration, label transfer, dynamic mapping, voting, refinement).

Unusually comprehensive experimental support: main comparisons against retrained LiDAR- and vision-based baselines, plus lighting-condition analysis (Table 5), component ablations (Table 4), and a strong supplementary with expert-count, FoV (90°–360°), bi-grid vs. single-grid, projection-path, resolution-scaling, calibration-noise, and temporal-aggregation ablations, plus on-device Jetson AGX Orin runtime measurements.
Baselines are retrained from scratch with documented, minimal, per-method adaptations (Tables 16–26), which improves fairness and reproducibility; the code/datasets are promised to be public.
The failure-case analysis (Sec. 12.2), range-wise safety analysis (Sec. 12.3), and honesty about limitations (single-campus QuadOcc, sim-to-real gap on H3O, single-frame design) are commendable.
weaknesses: The headline gains on the real benchmark are modest: +1.37 mIoU over MonoScene and +2.12 over LMSCNet on QuadOcc (Table 2), and the individual ablation increments are small (~+0.26 to +0.41 per component, Table 4). No variance across seeds or statistical significance is reported, so several component gains may be within training noise.

The Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) module regresses only a single global 2D offset (dx, dy) per scale/projection (Eqs. 9–10). Real gait-induced perturbation includes roll/pitch oscillation, non-rigid mounting flex, and local distortions that a global translation cannot model. The 'jitter-robust' claim is supported only indirectly (ablation gain of +0.39 and qualitative Fig. 8) rather than by a direct evaluation against measured jitter magnitude or motion state, weakening the central motivation.

The humanoid benchmark (H3O) simulates gait as a purely vertical sinusoidal bob (Eq. 24), which is a substantial simplification of real legged locomotion; conclusions about 'humanoid' robustness therefore carry a significant sim-to-real caveat that is acknowledged but undercuts the claimed scope.

Novelty of individual technical components is incremental: dual-encoder dual-projection fusion, cylindrical voxel grids (cf. Cylinder3D/PointOcc/OmniOcc), channel/spatial attention, MoE fusion, and a deformable sampling offset are each established ideas; the contribution is their combination and adaptation, not a fundamentally new mechanism. Notably, the paper does not empirically compare against the closest panoramic/cylindrical occupancy works it cites (e.g., OmniOcc [69], OccCylindrical [71]), which would strengthen the positioning.

Some baselines appear suspiciously weak after adaptation (e.g., VoxFormer-S at 9.36 mIoU on QuadOcc and 11.09 on H3O-Homo vs. MonoScene's 19.19/33.46), raising the possibility of under-tuned baseline adaptation, even though the adaptation protocol is documented.

The 'lightweight' framing is inconsistent with the numbers: the full QuadOcc configuration has 189.8M parameters, ~26% more than the MonoScene baseline (Table 13), and the Dual (ER+Raw) path costs +86.5% parameters and -14.8% throughput relative to ER-only (Table 9). Only the H3O configuration is genuinely lighter than the baseline.

QuadOcc ground truth is semi-automatic (multi-frame LiDAR aggregation + Grounded-SAM + manual fixes); the resulting label distribution and biases (e.g., toward LiDAR-observable static structure, ROAD dominance at 52%) are not analyzed for their effect on the LiDAR-vs-vision comparison, where the vision method claims to surpass LiDAR methods trained on the same labels.

The paper is heavily reliant on the supplementary for core justification (dataset construction, most ablations, runtime), which is acceptable for CVPR but means the main text alone provides limited depth on the strongest claims.
